entries.sentence: Epilepsy seizures are grouped by where they start in the brain and how much of it is involved.
entries.note: Returned summary: seizures classed by where they start and how much of the brain is involved; Epilepsy Action seizure pages.

entries.sentence: Focal seizures start in one area on one side of the brain, and some people stay aware during them while for others awareness is affected.
entries.note: Epilepsy Action focal seizures: start in one area on one side of the brain; awareness may be kept or affected.

entries.sentence: Generalised seizures involve both sides of the brain from the start, and a person does not usually stay conscious during them.
entries.note: Summary: generalised seizures involve both sides from the start; you do not usually stay conscious.

entries.sentence: Some people notice a warning before a seizure, called an aura.
entries.note: Summary: auras are warning sensations that often come before a seizure.

entries.sentence: An aura is usually a focal seizure in its own right.
entries.note: Summary: auras are usually a focal seizure in their own right.

entries.sentence: Examples include a strange feeling that is hard to describe, a rising feeling in the tummy, a feeling that events have happened before, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.
entries.note: Summary of NHS symptoms page: strange feeling, rising tummy feeling, deja vu, unusual smells or tastes, tingling in arms and legs.

entries.sentence: In a tonic-clonic seizure the person loses consciousness and the muscles go stiff, so someone who is standing may fall.
entries.note: Summary: tonic phase, you lose consciousness, muscles go stiff, may fall if standing.

entries.sentence: This is followed by repeated jerking of the arms or legs.
entries.note: Summary: the clonic phase brings repeated jerking of arms and/or legs.

entries.sentence: A seizure that begins on one side of the brain can also spread to both sides, which is called a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.
entries.note: Summary: focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures begin on one side and spread to both.

entries.sentence: Epilepsy Action advises seeing a GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure, even if you did not go to hospital at the time.
entries.note: Summary of Epilepsy Action diagnosis page: see your GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure even if you did not go to hospital.

entries.sentence: For a first suspected seizure, children over 2, young adults and adults should see an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks of the GP making the referral.
entries.note: Summary: specialist appointment within 2 weeks of GP referral for first suspected seizure; exact page carrying this not distinguished between Epilepsy Action and NICE.

entries.sentence: The GP may arrange some tests while you wait to see the specialist.
entries.note: Summary: your GP may be able to arrange some tests while you are waiting.

entries.sentence: No single test can confirm epilepsy.
entries.note: Summary: there is no single test that can confirm an epilepsy diagnosis.

entries.sentence: An EEG may be requested, and if it is done after a first seizure it should be done as soon as possible.
entries.note: Summary quoting NICE: if an EEG is requested after a first seizure it should be performed as soon as possible.

entries.sentence: A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, although a positive finding can support a provisional diagnosis.
entries.note: Summary quoting NICE: a negative routine EEG should not be used to exclude epilepsy, but a positive finding can support a provisional diagnosis.

entries.sentence: NICE recommends an MRI scan for most people who are diagnosed with epilepsy.
entries.note: Summary: NICE recommends MRI for most people diagnosed with epilepsy.

entries.sentence: An MRI scan cannot decide on its own whether someone has epilepsy, but together with other information it can help the clinician judge whether epilepsy is a likely cause.
entries.note: Summary: MRI cannot by itself determine epilepsy but with other information may help the clinician decide if epilepsy is a likely cause.

entries.sentence: Epilepsy Action advises keeping a seizure diary and taking it to the appointment.
entries.note: Summary: advice is to keep a seizure diary and take it to your appointment.

entries.sentence: If the diagnosis stays unclear, further investigations or referral to a specialist epilepsy centre should be considered.
entries.note: Summary quoting guidance: further investigations and/or referral to a tertiary epilepsy specialist should be considered if unclear.

entries.sentence: The NHS says anti-seizure medicines are the most commonly used treatment for epilepsy.
entries.note: Summary: NHS says anti-seizure medicines are most commonly used.

entries.sentence: They help control seizures in around 7 out of 10 people.
entries.note: Summary: NHS figure of around 7 out of 10 people.

entries.sentence: They do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening.
entries.note: Summary: do not cure epilepsy but can stop seizures happening.

entries.sentence: Some anti-seizure medicines can make some types of contraception, including the combined pill and implants, less effective, so this is worth raising with a doctor or nurse.
entries.note: Summary: NHS inform warns some ASMs can reduce effectiveness of some contraception including the combined pill and implants. The 'worth raising' wording is the author's framing.

entries.sentence: Other options are considered when medicines do not control the seizures.
entries.note: Summary of NHS treatment page and reviews: surgery, vagus nerve stimulation and ketogenic diet are non-drug options for hard-to-control epilepsy.

entries.sentence: Only a minority of people with hard-to-control epilepsy are candidates for traditional epilepsy surgery.
entries.note: Summary: only a minority of people with hard-to-control epilepsy are candidates for traditional surgery; source page not distinguished.

entries.sentence: Vagus nerve stimulation is another non-drug option that is used for epilepsy that has not responded to medicines.
entries.note: Summary: VNS listed as a non-drug option for drug-resistant epilepsy, approved for focal-onset drug-resistant epilepsy; mostly from research papers, not NHS page.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a ketogenic diet is sometimes recommended for children whose seizures are not controlled by medicines.
entries.note: Summary: NHS describes the ketogenic diet as sometimes recommended for children with seizures not controlled by anti-epileptic drugs.

entries.sentence: It should only be used under the supervision of an epilepsy specialist with the help of a dietitian.
entries.note: Summary: should only be used under supervision of an epilepsy specialist with help of a dietitian.

entries.sentence: NHS advice for a convulsive seizure is to support the person gently, cushion their head and not try to move them.
entries.note: Summary of NHS first-aid page: support gently and cushion their head, do not try to move them.

entries.sentence: The NHS also advises not putting anything in their mouth and not restraining them unless they are in immediate danger.
entries.note: Summary: don't put anything in their mouth and don't restrain unless in immediate danger.

entries.sentence: Once the convulsions stop, the advice is to place the person in the recovery position, stay with them and note when the seizure started and finished.
entries.note: Summary: once convulsions stop, recovery position, stay with them, note time seizure starts and finishes.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than is usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known.
entries.note: Summary: call for ambulance for first-time seizure, seizure longer than usual, or more than 5 minutes if pattern unknown.

entries.sentence: A 999 call is also advised if the person does not regain full consciousness, has several seizures without regaining consciousness, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing afterwards.
entries.note: Summary: also call if does not regain full consciousness, several seizures without regaining consciousness, seriously injured, trouble breathing afterwards.

entries.sentence: NHS inform describes status epilepticus, a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery in between, as a medical emergency.
entries.note: Summary: NHS Inform says status epilepticus is a seizure over 5 minutes or more than one seizure without regaining consciousness between, and is a medical emergency.

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests keeping a diary to spot triggers such as tiredness, stress, a period, flashing lights, food or drink.
entries.note: Summary: NHS suggests diary to spot triggers such as tiredness, stress, your period, flashing lights, food or drink; exact NHS page not confirmed.

entries.sentence: Epilepsy Action says that too little sleep or missing epilepsy medicines can lead to more seizures.
entries.note: Summary: lack of sleep or missing epilepsy medicines can cause an increase in seizures (Epilepsy Action safety/living pages).

entries.sentence: Some people find that stress-relieving activities such as exercise, yoga and meditation help.
entries.note: Summary: NHS 111 Wales suggests stress-relieving and relaxation therapies such as exercise, yoga and meditation may help.

entries.sentence: In the UK, the NHS says that a person must stop driving after any type of seizure and tell the DVLA.
entries.note: Summary: NHS says after any seizure you must stop driving and inform the DVLA.

entries.sentence: When driving can start again depends on the type of seizure and when it last happened.
entries.note: Summary: when you can start driving again depends on the seizure type and when it last happened.

entries.sentence: Epilepsy can also mean thinking carefully about certain jobs, swimming, contraception and planning a pregnancy.
entries.note: Summary of NHS 111 Wales: may have to think about epilepsy before driving, certain jobs, swimming, contraception and planning a pregnancy.

entries.sentence: For most people, an epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems.
entries.note: Summary of outlook text, attributed to NHS epilepsy pages; exact page not confirmed.

entries.sentence: The main risks are injury, seizures that go on for a long time and, rarely, sudden unexpected death in epilepsy.
entries.note: Summary: main risks are injury, prolonged seizures and rarely SUDEP.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes this sudden death as rare, and says epilepsy treatment can reduce the risk.
entries.note: Summary: NHS describes small risk of SUDEP, rare, and treatment can reduce it.

entries.sentence: The risk appears to be higher with frequent or poorly controlled seizures, which is why seizure control matters.
entries.note: Summary: risk appears higher with frequent or poorly controlled seizures; supported by research papers in results, Epilepsy Action page not confirmed.

entries.sentence: Anti-suffocation pillows have no research evidence that they reduce the risk.
entries.note: Summary: anti-suffocation pillows lack proof of benefit, no research to prove they reduce SUDEP risk; page not confirmed.

entries.sentence: The NHS says anti-seizure medicines do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening.
entries.note: Summary: do not cure epilepsy but can stop seizures.

entries.sentence: They help control seizures in around 7 out of 10 people.
entries.note: NHS figure around 7 out of 10.

entries.sentence: When medicines do not work well enough, other options such as surgery, nerve stimulation or a special diet may be discussed with an epilepsy specialist.
entries.note: Summary: surgery, VNS and ketogenic diet listed as options for hard-to-control epilepsy.

entries.note: Summary quoting NICE: negative routine EEG should not be used to exclude epilepsy.

entries.sentence: A positive result can support a provisional diagnosis, but no single test can confirm epilepsy.
entries.note: Summary: positive finding can support provisional diagnosis; no single test confirms epilepsy.

entries.sentence: Doctors weigh the EEG together with the story of what happened, any scan results and other information.
entries.note: Summary: MRI and other information considered together by the clinician; a seizure diary is useful. Paraphrased broadly.

entries.note: Summary noted these are UK rules and that rules differ in other countries.
